code.title: Index turns a full scan into a tree search
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE users(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT, city TEXT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO users(email, city) VALUES (?, ?)",
               [(f"user{i}@x.com", "Pune" if i % 2 else "Delhi") for i in range(1000)])

def plan(sql):
    # EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows whether the engine scans or searches
    return [r[3] for r in db.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN " + sql)]

q = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'user500@x.com'"
print("Rows:", db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users").fetchone()[0])
print("Before index:", plan(q))          # full scan, O(N)
db.execute("CREATE INDEX idx_email ON users(email)")
print("After index: ", plan(q))          # B-tree search, O(log N)
print("Result:", db.execute(q).fetchall())

followUps:
Put EXPLAIN (or EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN in SQLite) in front of the query and read the plan: SEARCH ... USING INDEX means an index is used, SCAN means every row is read.

Postgres: Index Scan or Seq Scan; EXPLAIN ANALYZE also runs the query and shows actual rows and time. MySQL shows the key column. Example: 1,000 rows, search by email: before the index SCAN users, after SEARCH users USING INDEX idx_email (email=?).

Usually yes: a primary key is backed by a unique index, so you do not need to create one yourself.

Postgres, MySQL and SQL Server all build it automatically to enforce uniqueness. In InnoDB and SQL Server the primary key is the clustered index, so the rows themselves are stored in key order. In SQLite an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is the rowid itself (no extra index); other primary keys get an automatic unique index. Foreign key columns are not indexed automatically in Postgres, so add those yourself.

code.title: Toy B+tree leaves: lookup and range scan
code.python:
import bisect

# Leaves hold sorted keys and are linked left to right.
keys = list(range(10, 100, 3))            # 10, 13, ..., 97
CAP = 4
leaves = [keys[i:i + CAP] for i in range(0, len(keys), CAP)]
firsts = [leaf[0] for leaf in leaves]     # separator keys (one "internal page")

def find_leaf(k):
    # follow one child pointer: the last leaf whose first key <= k
    return max(0, bisect.bisect_right(firsts, k) - 1)

def lookup(k):
    leaf = leaves[find_leaf(k)]
    i = bisect.bisect_left(leaf, k)       # binary search inside the leaf
    return i < len(leaf) and leaf[i] == k

def range_scan(lo, hi):
    out, li = [], find_leaf(lo)           # descend ONCE for the lower bound
    while li < len(leaves):               # then walk the leaf chain sideways
        for k in leaves[li]:
            if k > hi:
                return out
            if k >= lo:
                out.append(k)
        li += 1
    return out

print("Leaves:", leaves)
print("lookup(40):", lookup(40), " lookup(41):", lookup(41))
print("range 30..60:", range_scan(30, 60))

followUps:
A binary search tree holds one key per node and is tall, while a B+tree packs hundreds of keys into each disk page so it is very short.

With 1,000,000 keys a balanced binary tree is about 20 levels deep, so about 20 page reads from disk. A B+tree with fanout 200 needs only 3 levels (200 x 200 x 200 = 8,000,000). Disks read whole pages, so fewer levels means far fewer reads. Plain BSTs can also become unbalanced and degrade to O(N).

The leaf is split into two leaves and a separator key is pushed up to the parent, so the tree stays balanced.

Example with capacity 4: leaf [10, 20, 30, 40] receives 25. It becomes [10, 20] and [25, 30, 40], and the key 25 is copied into the parent. If the parent is full too, it splits the same way, and if the root splits a new root is created, so the tree grows at the top. Cost: a few extra page writes, which is why random inserts are costly.

In a B+tree all rows (or row pointers) live only in the linked leaves and internal nodes hold only separator keys; in a classic B-tree every node also stores data.

Consequences: B+tree internal pages hold more keys, so the tree is shorter. Every lookup ends at a leaf, so the time is predictable. Range scans just follow the leaf links, whereas a B-tree must move up and down the tree. Almost every database index called a B-tree is really a B+tree.

code.title: Clustered (rowid / WITHOUT ROWID) vs secondary index
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
# WITHOUT ROWID: the table itself is the B-tree ordered by the primary key (clustered)
db.execute("CREATE TABLE c(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, age INT) WITHOUT ROWID")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO c VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
               [(i, f"n{i}", 20 + i % 40) for i in range(1, 501)])
db.execute("CREATE INDEX idx_age ON c(age)")   # secondary: key + primary key

def plan(sql):
    return [r[3] for r in db.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN " + sql)]

print("By PK (rows live in the tree):", plan("SELECT * FROM c WHERE id = 42"))
print("By age (secondary, then PK hop):", plan("SELECT * FROM c WHERE age = 30"))
print("Covering age+id (no hop):      ", plan("SELECT id FROM c WHERE age = 30"))
print("Rows with age 30:", db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM c WHERE age = 30").fetchone()[0])

followUps:
Because every secondary index stores the primary key as its pointer, a big or random primary key is copied into every index and also causes page splits.

Example: a 16-byte UUID key plus 3 secondary indexes means 16 extra bytes in each index entry, fewer entries per page and a taller tree. A monotonically increasing 8-byte BIGINT appends at the right edge, pages stay nearly full, and the data is clustered by insert time, which matches how most tables are read.

CLUSTER table USING index rewrites the table once in the order of that index, but later inserts and updates are not kept in order.

Postgres tables are heaps: a new row goes wherever there is free space. Keeping physical order would require moving rows on every write, which costs too much. So the ordering decays and you must re-run CLUSTER, which takes an exclusive lock and rewrites the whole table. Use it for read-mostly tables, or use pg_repack online.

code.title: Left-prefix rule on index (a, b, c)
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE t(a INT, b INT, c INT, pad TEXT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO t VALUES (?, ?, ?, 'x')",
               [(i % 20, i % 7, i % 5) for i in range(2000)])
db.execute("CREATE INDEX idx_abc ON t(a, b, c)")
db.execute("ANALYZE")

def plan(where):
    sql = "SELECT pad FROM t WHERE " + where
    return [r[3] for r in db.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN " + sql)][0]

# Only a leading run of columns can be sought
for w in ["a = 3", "a = 3 AND b = 2", "a = 3 AND b = 2 AND c = 1",
          "b = 2", "c = 1", "a = 3 AND c = 1", "a > 5 AND b = 2"]:
    print(f"{w:28} -> {plan(w)}")

followUps:
Put the columns used with equality first, then the ORDER BY column, then range columns (ESR).

Example: WHERE tenant_id = ? AND status = ? ORDER BY created_at gets index (tenant_id, status, created_at). The seek lands on one block (tenant, status) already sorted by created_at, so no sort is needed. If you put the range column earlier, the later columns can no longer be sought. Among equalities, prefer the column shared by most queries first.

Yes, (a, b) makes an index on (a) redundant, because (a, b) is also sorted by a; it does not make (b) redundant.

Queries on a alone can use the (a, b) index with a seek, so a separate (a) index only costs writes and space (it is a bit smaller, which is the rare exception). A query on b alone cannot seek on (a, b), so if you filter by b you need a separate index on b. Drop the redundant left-prefix index after checking plans.

code.title: ESR: equality, sort, range column order
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE ev(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, tenant_id INT, status TEXT, created_at INT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO ev(tenant_id, status, created_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
               [(i % 10, "open" if i % 3 else "done", i) for i in range(3000)])
q = ("SELECT * FROM ev WHERE tenant_id = 3 AND status = 'open' AND created_at > 500 "
     "ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 5")

def plan():
    return [r[3] for r in db.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN " + q)]

# Weaker: the range column sits before status, so status cannot be sought
db.execute("CREATE INDEX bad ON ev(tenant_id, created_at, status)")
print("Order (E, R, E), status not sought:", plan())
db.execute("DROP INDEX bad")
# Good: Equality, Equality, then the column used for both sort and range
db.execute("CREATE INDEX good ON ev(tenant_id, status, created_at)")
print("Order ESR:      ", plan())
print("Rows:", len(db.execute(q).fetchall()))

followUps:
Use (tenant_id, status, created_at): two equalities first, then the column used for both the range and the sort.

CREATE INDEX ix ON t(tenant_id, status, created_at);
SELECT * FROM t
WHERE tenant_id = ? AND status = ? AND created_at > ?
ORDER BY created_at;

The seek jumps to (tenant, status, created_at > ?) and reads forward in sorted order, so no sort step is needed. The range and the sort are on the same column, so they fit together.

A normal index cannot serve mixed directions unless the index itself is declared with the same mix, for example (a ASC, b DESC).

An index scanned forward gives a ASC, b ASC and scanned backward gives a DESC, b DESC, but never a ASC with b DESC. Without a matching index the engine adds a sort step. Postgres, SQL Server, MySQL 8 and SQLite all let you write CREATE INDEX ix ON t(a ASC, b DESC), after which the query is served in order.

code.title: Covering index avoids table lookups
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE u(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT, name TEXT, bio TEXT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO u(email, name, bio) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
               [(f"e{i}@x.com", f"name{i}", "long text " * 20) for i in range(500)])

def plan(sql):
    return [r[3] for r in db.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN " + sql)][0]

q = "SELECT name FROM u WHERE email = 'e10@x.com'"
db.execute("CREATE INDEX i_email ON u(email)")
print("email only:     ", plan(q))              # index, then fetch row for name
db.execute("CREATE INDEX i_email_name ON u(email, name)")
print("email, name:    ", plan(q))              # COVERING INDEX: no table read
print("SELECT *:       ", plan("SELECT * FROM u WHERE email = 'e10@x.com'"))
print("Result:", db.execute(q).fetchall())

followUps:
Because the index only holds a visibility hint per page, and when a page is not marked all-visible Postgres must check the table row to see whether the row is visible to your transaction.

Visibility info (MVCC) lives in the heap. The visibility map marks pages where all rows are visible to everyone; recently changed pages are not marked until VACUUM runs. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows Heap Fetches: N; if N is large, vacuum the table more often.

No: in InnoDB every secondary index automatically contains the primary key columns at the end of each entry, so they are always available for covering.

Example: INDEX (email) on a table with PK id covers SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = ? without any extra column. MySQL has no INCLUDE clause; to cover other columns you append them as normal key columns, which affects ordering and size.

code.title: Hash lookup vs ordered (B-tree-like) structure
code.python:
import bisect

keys = [40, 10, 30, 20, 50, 60, 70]
hash_index = {k: f"row{k}" for k in keys}      # O(1) average equality
sorted_keys = sorted(keys)                     # ordered, like a B-tree leaf level

print("Keys:", keys)
print("Equality 30 via hash:  ", hash_index.get(30))

def range_scan(lo, hi):
    i = bisect.bisect_left(sorted_keys, lo)    # O(log N) to find the start
    out = []
    while i < len(sorted_keys) and sorted_keys[i] <= hi:
        out.append(sorted_keys[i])
        i += 1
    return out

print("Range 20..50 via sorted:", range_scan(20, 50))
# A hash has no order: a range needs a full scan of every key, O(N)
print("Range 20..50 via hash:  ", sorted(k for k in hash_index if 20 <= k <= 50), "(scanned all)")
print("MIN via sorted:", sorted_keys[0], " MIN via hash: needs full scan ->", min(hash_index))

followUps:
Hash joins and hash aggregation (GROUP BY or DISTINCT) build in-memory hash tables during execution, even if no hash index exists.

Example: joining 1M orders with 10k customers, the engine builds a hash table of the 10k customers and probes it once per order row, about O(N + M) work instead of nested loops. These hash tables are temporary and per query, unlike a stored hash index, and they spill to disk when they exceed the work memory.

Use a GIN index for JSONB containment (and arrays or full-text), and an approximate-nearest-neighbour index such as HNSW or IVFFlat for vector similarity.

Example in Postgres: CREATE INDEX ON docs USING gin (data jsonb_path_ops) speeds data @> '{"tag":"x"}'. For embeddings, pgvector offers USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops) for ORDER BY embedding <=> ?. A B-tree cannot answer these queries.

code.title: Selectivity decides if an index is worth using
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE o(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, status TEXT)")
# 10000 rows: 'done' is common, 'failed' is rare (skewed column)
rows = ["failed" if i % 500 == 0 else "done" for i in range(10000)]
db.executemany("INSERT INTO o(status) VALUES (?)", [(s,) for s in rows])
db.execute("CREATE INDEX i_status ON o(status)")
db.execute("ANALYZE")                           # gather statistics for the planner

total = len(rows)
for s, n in db.execute("SELECT status, COUNT(*) FROM o GROUP BY status"):
    print(f"{s:7} matches {n:5} rows = selectivity {n / total:.2%}")
print("Distinct values (cardinality):", db.execute("SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT status) FROM o").fetchone()[0])

def plan(v):
    sql = f"SELECT * FROM o WHERE status = '{v}'"
    return [r[3] for r in db.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN " + sql)][0]

print("failed ->", plan("failed"))
print("done   ->", plan("done"))

followUps:
Usually no, because a boolean has only 2 values, so each value matches a large share of the rows and the planner will mostly ignore the index.

Exception: a skewed column, such as 99.9% false and 0.1% true. Then WHERE is_active = true returns 10 of 10,000 rows and an index helps. Even better is a partial index ON t(id) WHERE flag, which stores only the rare rows and is tiny.

Parameter sniffing is when the engine builds one plan using the first parameter value it sees and then reuses it for all values, even when that plan is wrong for them.

With skew, status 'failed' matches 20 rows (index seek is best) and 'done' matches 9,980 rows (scan is best). If the plan is first compiled for 'failed' and cached, 'done' runs a slow 9,980-row seek loop. Fixes: OPTION (RECOMPILE), OPTIMIZE FOR, or separate queries for the rare and common value.

code.title: Non-sargable predicates ignore the index
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE p(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT, age INT, code TEXT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO p(email, age, code) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
               [(f"User{i}@X.com", i % 90, str(i)) for i in range(2000)])
db.execute("CREATE INDEX i_email ON p(email)")
db.execute("CREATE INDEX i_age ON p(age)")

def plan(where):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM p WHERE " + where
    return [r[3] for r in db.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN " + sql)][0]

tests = [
    "email = 'User5@X.com'",          # sargable
    "lower(email) = 'user5@x.com'",   # function on the column
    "email LIKE '%X.com'",            # leading wildcard
    "age + 1 = 31",                   # arithmetic on the column
    "age = 30",                       # rewritten: sargable
    "age = 30 OR email = 'a'",        # OR across columns
]
for w in tests:
    print(f"{w:32} -> {plan(w)}")

followUps:
Use a hint or a setting, to see what the planner does when it is forced; do it only for a quick experiment.

SQLite: SELECT * FROM t INDEXED BY idx WHERE .... Postgres: SET enable_seqscan = off; in your session, then re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE. MySQL: FORCE INDEX (idx). SQL Server: WITH (INDEX(idx)). If the forced plan is much faster, the statistics or cost estimates are wrong; if it is slower, the planner was right.

Because the data changes, and a forced plan that was best today can become the worst tomorrow, while the planner cannot adapt.

Example: forcing an index that suits 1% of rows is fine, until growth or new data makes the filter match 40% of the table. The forced seek loop now does millions of random reads, but the planner is not allowed to switch to a scan. A hint also fails if the index is renamed or dropped. Fix the root cause: statistics, the query, or the index design.

code.title: More indexes mean more storage and write work
code.python:
import sqlite3, time

def build(extra_indexes):
    db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    db.execute("CREATE TABLE t(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, a INT, b INT, c INT, d INT)")
    for i, col in enumerate("abcd"[:extra_indexes]):
        db.execute(f"CREATE INDEX i{i} ON t({col})")
    # pseudo-random values so index inserts land all over the trees
    rows = [((i * 7919) % 10007, (i * 104729) % 10009, (i * 15485863) % 10037, i)
            for i in range(20000)]
    start = time.perf_counter()
    db.executemany("INSERT INTO t(a, b, c, d) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)", rows)
    db.commit()
    secs = time.perf_counter() - start
    pages = db.execute("PRAGMA page_count").fetchone()[0]
    return pages, secs

base_pages, base_t = build(0)
for n in (0, 2, 4):
    pages, secs = build(n)
    print(f"{n} secondary indexes: {pages:5} pages ({pages / base_pages:.1f}x size), "
          f"insert time {secs / base_t:.1f}x of baseline")
# Timing varies per machine, but size and write cost grow with every index.

followUps:
Check the usage counters the engine keeps: an index with zero scans over a long period is a candidate.

Postgres: SELECT indexrelname, idx_scan FROM pg_stat_user_indexes WHERE idx_scan = 0; (ignore unique and primary key indexes, which enforce constraints). MySQL: SELECT * FROM sys.schema_unused_indexes;. Counters reset on restart or stats reset, so observe a full business cycle (month-end jobs!) and check replicas too.

Make it invisible or measure first, then drop it with a non-blocking command, and keep the definition so you can recreate it.

Steps: (1) save the CREATE INDEX DDL; (2) in MySQL 8 run ALTER INDEX ix INVISIBLE and watch latency for a week; (3) Postgres: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY ix; which avoids a long lock; (4) if queries slow down, recreate it with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.

code.title: Random vs sequential keys: leaf fill and page splits
code.python:
import random, bisect

CAP = 8

def insert_all(keys):
    leaves = [[]]                        # sorted leaves, each holds up to CAP keys
    splits = 0
    for k in keys:
        firsts = [l[0] if l else -1 for l in leaves]
        i = max(0, bisect.bisect_right(firsts, k) - 1)
        bisect.insort(leaves[i], k)
        if len(leaves[i]) > CAP:
            splits += 1
            if i == len(leaves) - 1 and leaves[i][-1] == k:
                leaves.append([leaves[i].pop()])      # append at right edge: new page
            else:
                half = len(leaves[i]) // 2           # middle split leaves pages half full
                leaves.insert(i + 1, leaves[i][half:])
                leaves[i] = leaves[i][:half]
    fill = sum(len(l) for l in leaves) / (len(leaves) * CAP)
    return len(leaves), splits, fill

random.seed(1)
n = 2000
seq = list(range(n))
rnd = seq[:]
random.shuffle(rnd)                      # like UUIDv4 order
for name, keys in (("sequential", seq), ("random UUIDv4-like", rnd)):
    pages, splits, fill = insert_all(keys)
    print(f"{name:18}: {pages} pages, {splits} splits, avg fill {fill:.0%}")

followUps:
All inserts hit the same last leaf page, so many sessions fight over one hot page and its latch, which limits write throughput.

Example: 10,000 inserts per second with an auto-increment key all append to the right edge. The page fills, splits, and every thread waits for the same lock. Fixes: spread the load with partitioning, hash-prefixed or sharded keys, or batch the inserts. Sequential keys are a great default; this only matters at very high write rates.

Spanner stores rows ordered by key and splits ranges across servers, so a sequential key sends all writes to one server; it avoids this by recommending keys that are not monotonic.

Examples: use a UUIDv4, bit-reverse a sequence value, or prefix the key with a hash shard such as shard = hash(id) % 16. Writes then spread over many splits, and Spanner can also split a hot range automatically.

code.title: Partial index and expression index
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE j(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, status TEXT, created INT, email TEXT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO j(status, created, email) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
               [("pending" if i % 100 == 0 else "done", i, f"User{i}@X.com") for i in range(5000)])

def plan(sql):
    return [r[3] for r in db.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN " + sql)][0]

# Partial: indexes only the ~1% of rows that are pending
db.execute("CREATE INDEX i_pending ON j(created) WHERE status = 'pending'")
n = db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM j WHERE status = 'pending'").fetchone()[0]
print("Pending rows indexed:", n, "of 5000")
print("pending query:", plan("SELECT * FROM j WHERE status = 'pending' ORDER BY created"))
print("done query:   ", plan("SELECT * FROM j WHERE status = 'done' ORDER BY created"))

q = "SELECT * FROM j WHERE lower(email) = 'user7@x.com'"
print("Before expression index:", plan(q))
db.execute("CREATE INDEX i_lower ON j(lower(email))")   # index the computed value
print("After expression index: ", plan(q))
print("Match:", db.execute(q).fetchall())

followUps:
Because with a prepared statement the plan is built before the value is known, and the planner cannot prove the generic condition implies the index predicate.

Index: WHERE status = 'pending'. Query WHERE status = $1 could be any status, so a generic plan cannot use the index. Fixes: write the literal into the query (status = 'pending'), or let Postgres use a custom plan per value (plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan).

Store the value in lower case, or use a case-insensitive type or collation, so a plain index works.

Options: (1) Postgres citext column, then a normal index on email; (2) a deterministic case-insensitive collation; (3) a generated column email_lc holding lower(email) with a normal index (the way MySQL does it); (4) SQLite COLLATE NOCASE on the column and index. All avoid repeating the expression in every query.

code.title: Slow endpoint: EXPLAIN, fix, verify
code.python:
import sqlite3, time

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT, status TEXT, total REAL)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO orders(customer_id, status, total) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
               [(i % 2000, "paid", i * 0.5) for i in range(100000)])
q = "SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1234 ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 5"

def plan():
    return [r[3] for r in db.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN " + q)]

def timed():
    t = time.perf_counter()
    rows = db.execute(q).fetchall()
    return rows, (time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000

rows, ms = timed()
print("1. Plan before:", plan())                 # step 1-2: find the scan
db.execute("CREATE INDEX i_cust ON orders(customer_id)")   # step 4: minimal fix
print("2. Plan after: ", plan())                 # step 5: verify the plan changed
rows2, ms2 = timed()
print("3. Same rows before and after:", rows == rows2)
print("4. Faster after index:", ms2 < ms)

followUps:
Copy production's shape, not its secrets: restore a recent backup (masked) or generate data of the same size and the same value skew.

Plans depend on row counts and statistics, so 1,000 rows will pick a scan where 100 million rows would pick the index. Steps: load comparable data, run ANALYZE, compare EXPLAIN ANALYZE before and after, and test the writes too. Also try a read replica or a snapshot clone of production.

Fix it at the database level instead: add or change indexes for the SQL the ORM generates, and capture the real query text first.

Steps: log the generated SQL (slow query log or APM), find N+1 patterns, and create the index that matches it. In the ORM you can often still add eager loading (select_related, Include), a projection to select fewer columns, or a raw-SQL escape hatch for the worst query. Index fixes need no code change.

code.title: Index order serves ORDER BY ... LIMIT
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE m(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, user_id INT, ts INT, body TEXT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO m(user_id, ts, body) VALUES (?, ?, 'x')",
               [(i % 50, i) for i in range(5000)])

def plan(sql):
    return [r[3] for r in db.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN " + sql)]

q = "SELECT * FROM m WHERE user_id = 7 ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 3"
db.execute("CREATE INDEX i_user ON m(user_id)")
print("Index on user_id only:", plan(q))          # needs a temp sort
db.execute("CREATE INDEX i_user_ts ON m(user_id, ts)")
print("Index on (user_id, ts):", plan(q))         # reads in order, stops after 3
print("Rows:", [r[2] for r in db.execute(q)])

g = "SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) FROM m GROUP BY user_id"
print("GROUP BY plan:", plan(g))                  # streams groups from the index

followUps:
Because OFFSET 100000 still has to walk past and throw away 100,000 index entries before returning the page, so the cost grows with the page number.

Keyset pagination remembers the last row and seeks there: WHERE (ts, id) < (?, ?) ORDER BY ts DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20. With an index on (ts, id) every page costs the same, O(log N + 20), not O(offset + 20). The trade-off: no jumping to an arbitrary page number.

Rarely: a hash index has no order, so it cannot return rows sorted and ORDER BY still needs a sort.

The only help is indirect: a hash index may find the matching rows for WHERE k = ? quickly, but the engine must then sort them, with cost O(M log M) for M matches. If M is small that is fine. Use a B-tree on (k, sort_col) to get the rows already in order.
